title: GOD HEARD SARAH LAUGH BEHIND THE TENT—THEN ASKED ONE QUESTION THAT STILL SHAKES HEAVEN AND EARTH
paragraphs: GOD HEARD SARAH LAUGH BEHIND THE TENT—THEN ASKED ONE QUESTION THAT STILL SHAKES HEAVEN AND EARTH

“Is Anything Too Hard for the LORD?” — Genesis 18:14 | The heartbreaking story of a woman who stopped expecting a miracle, a God who never forgot His promise, and the grace that reaches us even when our faith has grown tired.
What if the prayer you stopped praying is the very prayer God has not forgotten?
What if the dream you buried, the tears you wiped away when nobody was watching, and the promise you no longer dare to mention are not nearly as hidden from God as you think?
And what if, at the very moment you have convinced yourself that nothing will ever change, heaven is asking you the same question it once asked a woman who laughed behind a tent?
“Is any thing too hard for the LORD?” — Genesis 18:14 (KJV)
Before you answer, you need to understand something.
God did not ask that question in a palace surrounded by people celebrating answered prayers.
He asked it in the middle of an ordinary day, near an ordinary tent, where an elderly woman had learned to live with an extraordinary disappointment.
Her name was Sarah.
And she had no idea that the laughter she thought nobody heard would become part of one of the most unforgettable conversations in Scripture.
Because sometimes the deepest crisis of faith does not sound like someone shouting, “God, I don't believe You!”
Sometimes it sounds like a quiet laugh from someone who has been disappointed for so long that hope itself feels dangerous.
Sarah knew that kind of disappointment.
She knew what it meant to watch the years pass while the promise remained unfulfilled.
She knew what it meant to grow older while other families welcomed children.
She knew what it meant to carry a longing that no amount of explanation could erase.
And perhaps that is why her story feels so painfully familiar.
Because there are people reading this who still attend church, still worship, still open their Bibles, still tell others that God is faithful...
But somewhere deep inside, there is a prayer they have stopped bringing before Him.
Not necessarily because they stopped believing in God.
But because they are afraid of hoping again.
And that is where this story begins to reach into places we would rather keep hidden.
Genesis 18 tells us that the LORD appeared to Abraham near the great trees of Mamre.
Abraham was sitting at the entrance of his tent during the heat of the day when he saw three visitors standing nearby.
He hurried to welcome them.
Water was brought. Food was prepared. Hospitality was offered.
What appeared to be an ordinary encounter became the setting for a divine announcement.
One of the visitors declared:
“I will certainly return unto thee according to the time of life; and, lo, Sarah thy wife shall have a son.” — Genesis 18:10 (KJV)
Sarah was listening from the tent entrance behind him.
She was ninety years old, according to Genesis 17:17.
Abraham was about one hundred.
Genesis 18:11 does not soften the biological reality. Abraham and Sarah were old, and Sarah was past the age of childbearing.
This was not a promise that merely required better circumstances.
Humanly speaking, the opportunity had passed.
And Sarah knew it.
She had lived in that body.
She had watched those years disappear.
She understood the difference between what she wanted and what seemed physically possible.
So when she heard that she would have a son, she laughed within herself.
Not the joyful laughter of a mother holding her newborn.
Not yet.
It was the laughter of someone who could no longer reconcile the promise with the reality standing in front of her.
Genesis 18:12 records her private response:
“Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?” (KJV)
Imagine that moment.
An aging woman standing where she believed nobody could see what was happening inside her.
A promise she had carried for decades suddenly being spoken aloud again.
And instead of excitement, something inside her recoiled.
Perhaps you understand.
You have heard sermons about restoration while your family remains divided.
You have listened to testimonies of healing while your own suffering continues.
You have celebrated other people's breakthroughs while quietly wondering whether yours will ever come.
You have watched doors open for people who seemed to arrive long after you began waiting.
And although you would never say it publicly, there have been moments when the language of miracles felt almost unbearable.
Because it is difficult to keep expecting something when the evidence around you seems to be moving in the opposite direction.
But here is where the story becomes astonishing.
Sarah laughed within herself.
And God heard her.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 18:12 says:
וַתִּצְחַק שָׂרָה בְּקִרְבָּהּ
Vattitschaq Sarah beqirbah.
A faithful translation is:
“And Sarah laughed within herself.”
The Hebrew expression beqirbah communicates that this laughter occurred inwardly, within her.
It was not a public speech.
It was not a confession made before an audience.
Yet the LORD knew.
And this matters because God does not merely hear the words we are brave enough to pray.
He knows the thoughts we are afraid to admit.
He sees the exhaustion beneath our religious language.
He knows when our confidence is genuine and when we are simply trying to survive another day without falling apart.
Then came the question.
The LORD said to Abraham:
“Wherefore did Sarah laugh, saying, Shall I of a surety bear a child, which am old?” — Genesis 18:13 (KJV)
And immediately afterward:
“Is any thing too hard for the LORD?” — Genesis 18:14 (KJV)
Read that again.
God did not ask Sarah whether she understood reproductive biology.
He did not deny her age.
He did not pretend that the circumstances were normal.
He confronted the assumption that those circumstances could place a limit on His ability to fulfill what He had promised.
And the original Hebrew makes the question even more striking.
הֲיִפָּלֵא מֵיְהוָה דָּבָר
Hayyippale meYHWH davar?
Literally, the question carries the sense:
“Is a thing too extraordinary or too difficult for the LORD?”
The Hebrew verb comes from the root פלא (p-l-ʾ), associated with what is extraordinary, wonderful, or beyond ordinary human ability.
The word davar can mean a word, matter, or thing, depending on context.
Here the question concerns whether the promised event is beyond the LORD's power.
It is not simply an invitation to positive thinking.
It is a revelation of who God is.
The question is not whether Sarah possesses enough emotional strength to manufacture a miracle.
The question is whether the LORD is capable of accomplishing what He Himself has spoken.
And the answer is unmistakable.
No.
Nothing God has promised is beyond His power to accomplish.
But we must understand this carefully.
Genesis 18:14 does not mean that every personal desire will eventually happen if we believe hard enough.
It does not mean every sickness will disappear in this life, every broken relationship will be restored on our preferred schedule, or every financial difficulty will end through a sudden miracle.
God's omnipotence is not a blank check for our expectations.
The promise to Sarah was a specific divine promise within God's unfolding covenant with Abraham.
And that distinction does not weaken the passage.
It makes it more glorious.
Because the deepest message is not that God must accomplish everything we want.
It is that God is utterly faithful to accomplish everything He has promised.
And the God who keeps His word is worthy of our trust even when His timing remains painful.
But there is something else in this story that we cannot afford to overlook.
Sarah's laughter did not happen in isolation.
Years earlier, God had promised Abraham descendants and a covenant future.
Yet Sarah remained barren.
The waiting became so painful that Genesis 16 records a devastating attempt to obtain the promised family through human arrangements.
Sarah gave her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham as a wife, hoping to build a family through her.
Hagar conceived.
And the household fractured.
Jealousy followed.
Harsh treatment followed.
Hagar suffered.
The consequences were real, and Scripture does not invite us to ignore them.
This was not a beautiful shortcut to God's promise.
It was a deeply troubled human decision that wounded vulnerable people.
And still, God did not abandon His covenant purpose.
That does not mean He approved of everything Abraham and Sarah did.
It means human failure did not overpower His faithfulness.
Even in Genesis 16, the LORD saw Hagar in her distress.
The God who remembered Sarah's future also saw the suffering of the woman caught in the consequences of that household's decisions.
This is important.
Because biblical grace never requires us to pretend that sin does not harm people.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace tells the truth about what happened while revealing that God is still able to act with mercy and righteousness.
Some of us know exactly what it means to create additional pain while trying to escape the pain of waiting.
We forced a relationship because we were afraid of being alone.
We compromised our convictions because we feared losing an opportunity.
We made a decision out of desperation and then spent years living with its consequences.
We tried to control what we were supposed to entrust to God.
And afterward, shame began whispering that our failures had disqualified us from ever being used by Him again.
But look at Abraham and Sarah.
Their history was complicated.
Their decisions were imperfect.
Their household had suffered.
Yet God was still faithful to His covenant.
Not because their mistakes were harmless.
Not because their faith was flawless.
But because His faithfulness was greater than their failures.
And if you are reading this while carrying regret over decisions you cannot undo, please hear this carefully:
Repentance does not erase every earthly consequence, but failure does not place a repentant sinner beyond the mercy of God.
That mercy finds its fullest revelation in Jesus Christ.
But before we reach the cross, we need to return to the tent.
Because Sarah had been listening.
She had laughed.
God had confronted the laughter.
And now she was afraid.
Genesis 18:15 says:
“Then Sarah denied, saying, I laughed not; for she was afraid. And he said, Nay; but thou didst laugh.” (KJV)
There it is.
A painfully human moment.
She laughed.
She was confronted.
She became afraid.
And she denied what she had done.
How often have we followed that same pattern?
We doubt, then hide the doubt.
We sin, then defend ourselves.
We become bitter, then insist that we are fine.
We carry resentment, then cover it with religious language.
We tell people that everything is wonderful because we are terrified of what they might think if they knew how deeply we were struggling.
Sarah's response was not courageous.
It was not honest.
But it was human.
And God's reply was direct.
“No, you did laugh.”
He did not allow her denial to rewrite the truth.
Yet the narrative does not end with Sarah being discarded.
That is one of the most moving details in the entire account.
God exposed the truth without abandoning His promise.
His correction did not mean that His covenant faithfulness had expired.
There is a lesson here for everyone who has confused divine correction with divine rejection.
God's Word can confront us precisely because His truth is not indifferent to what is happening in our hearts.
And for those who belong to Christ, correction can be an expression of a Father's loving discipline, not a declaration that redemption has failed.
Sometimes the truth we most need is the truth we have spent the longest avoiding.
Perhaps you have been pretending you are spiritually healthy when your prayer life has quietly collapsed.
Perhaps you have been hiding a habit you know is pulling your heart away from God.
Perhaps you have been blaming everyone else because admitting your own responsibility would require repentance.
Perhaps your struggle is not rebellion at all, but the quiet exhaustion of someone who has suffered for years.
Those situations are not identical, and they should not be treated as though they are.
But none of them needs to be hidden behind a false appearance of perfection.
God already knows the truth.
The invitation is to come into the light.
To confess what needs confession.
To seek help where help is needed.
To grieve honestly.
To stop pretending that spiritual maturity means never struggling.
And to remember that Jesus did not come to save people who could successfully conceal their need for a Savior.
He came to save sinners.
Now consider what happened next.
Genesis 21 opens with words that must have sounded almost impossible to Sarah only a short time earlier.
“And the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken.” — Genesis 21:1 (KJV)
Notice the repetition.
As He had said.
As He had spoken.
The emphasis is not on Sarah's ability to maintain perfect optimism.
It is on God's faithfulness to His word.
Then the impossible became visible.
Sarah conceived.
She bore Abraham a son in his old age.
And Abraham named him Isaac.
In Hebrew, Isaac's name is יִצְחָק (Yitschaq), associated with the verb meaning “to laugh.”
Think about that.
The woman who had laughed in disbelief was now holding a child whose very name recalled laughter.
Genesis 21:6 records Sarah saying:
“God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me.” (KJV)
What an extraordinary transformation.
In Genesis 18, laughter revealed her struggle to believe the announcement.
In Genesis 21, laughter expressed her joy at its fulfillment.
The same woman.
The same God.
But an entirely different moment.
The years had not been imaginary.
The waiting had not been easy.
The mistakes had not been erased from history.
Yet the promise had come to pass.
And the laughter that once accompanied her disbelief now accompanied her astonishment.
This is where the story becomes even more beautiful.
Because Isaac was not merely the answer to an elderly couple's desire for a child.
He belonged to a covenant story that would eventually lead us to Jesus Christ.
God had promised Abraham that through his offspring the nations of the earth would be blessed.
The covenant continued through Isaac and Jacob, through Israel's history, and ultimately toward the Messiah.
The New Testament draws our attention to this larger fulfillment.
Galatians 3:16 identifies Christ as the ultimate promised offspring through whom the covenant blessing reaches its goal.
And Galatians 3:29 teaches that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise.
That does not mean every detail of Sarah's experience becomes a guarantee of identical circumstances for every Christian.
It means her story belongs to something far greater than her personal breakthrough.
The God who brought Isaac into the world was moving history toward the coming of His Son.
And when we understand that, Genesis 18:14 begins to shine with a deeper light.
Because the question, “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” does not reach its greatest significance merely in the birth of Isaac.
It points us toward the faithfulness and saving power of the God who would send Jesus Christ.
Centuries later, another woman would hear an astonishing announcement concerning the birth of a son.
Mary was told that she would conceive Jesus through the power of the Holy Spirit.
Her circumstances were not the same as Sarah's.
Sarah was an elderly married woman beyond childbearing age.
Mary was a virgin.
Their responses were also different.
But both accounts reveal God's power to accomplish what human ability cannot produce.
And in Luke 1:37, the angel declares:
“For with God nothing shall be impossible.” (KJV)
The Greek reads:
ὅτι οὐκ ἀδυνατήσει παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πᾶν ῥῆμα
Hoti ouk adynatēsei para tou theou pan rhēma.
The expression can be understood as affirming that no word or promise from God will prove powerless or impossible.
This fits the context: God will accomplish what He has announced.
The connection is breathtaking.
The God who fulfilled His promise concerning Isaac would fulfill His greater saving purpose through Jesus.
And Jesus did not enter this world merely to inspire us to dream bigger.
He came because our greatest problem was deeper than disappointment.
Our greatest problem was sin.
We were not simply people waiting for better circumstances.
We were people in need of reconciliation with a holy God.
Romans 3:23 tells us that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
Romans 6:23 declares that the wages of sin is death, but God's gift is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
And Romans 5:8 announces the heart of the Gospel:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
There is the miracle we must never overlook.
The Son of God took on human flesh.
He lived without sin.
He bore our sins in His death upon the cross.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day.
The resurrection was not a metaphor for personal improvement.
It was God's decisive victory over death and the vindication of His Son.
And through the crucified and risen Christ, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to sinners who repent and believe.
That is why the Christian message cannot be reduced to “Your miracle is coming.”
Sometimes the earthly miracle we long for does not come in the way we hoped.
Some faithful believers die without seeing a particular prayer answered as they desired.
Some families continue to grieve.
Some illnesses remain.
Some wounds require years of healing, wise care, and patient support.
And some losses will not be reversed before the resurrection.
But the Gospel gives us a hope deeper than the guarantee of immediate relief.
Because even when God does not change our circumstances according to our timetable, Jesus Christ has already accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
He has opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
And He promises a future in which death itself will not have the final word.
This is why the cross matters more than any temporary breakthrough.
The greatest evidence of God's love is not that every painful situation turns out exactly as we requested.
It is that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
And the greatest proof that death does not have ultimate authority is the empty tomb.
So when we return to the question asked near Abraham's tent, we must hear it in the light of the whole biblical story.
“Is anything too hard for the LORD?”
Not the barrenness of Sarah.
Not the impossible circumstances surrounding the promised birth of Isaac.
Not the centuries of history through which God preserved His redemptive purpose.
Not the grave that could not hold the risen Christ.
And not the guilt of a sinner who comes to Jesus in genuine repentance and faith.
Perhaps that last truth is the one you most desperately need.
Because maybe your deepest struggle is not that you doubt God can change your circumstances.
Maybe you doubt that He could still receive someone like you.
You remember the lies.
The compromises.
The betrayal.
The addiction.
The secret conversations.
The anger you justified.
The people you hurt.
The years you wasted.
The opportunities you threw away.
And you have begun to believe that your story has become too stained for grace.
But the Gospel confronts that despair.
Jesus Christ did not die for an imaginary humanity with imaginary sins.
He died to save real sinners.
People with histories.
People with shame.
People who have no righteousness of their own to offer Him.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not to make yourself worthy before coming to Christ.
It is to repent and trust in the Savior who alone is worthy.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That is not permission to continue in deliberate rebellion.
Grace is not an excuse to remain enslaved to the very sin from which Christ came to save us.
True faith turns toward Christ, and genuine repentance involves turning away from sin.
The Christian life is not sinless perfection in this present age, but it is a life being transformed by the grace of God.
And perhaps that is the moment your story begins to change.
Not when every external problem disappears.
Not when everyone finally understands you.
Not when the past can somehow be undone.
But when you stop running from the Savior who already knows the truth about you.
When you finally say:
“Lord Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“I have been trying to carry what I cannot carry.”
“I have called myself hopeless when Your Word calls me to repentance and faith.”
“I have looked at my failures more than I have looked at Your cross.”
“Have mercy on me.”
And if those words are close to what your heart has been trying to say, you do not need to wait for a perfect moment to pray.
You can turn to Christ now.
Not because this article has power to save you.
But because Jesus Christ is the Savior, and salvation is God's gift of grace received through faith.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
And if you already belong to Christ but have grown exhausted, hear this too.
Your faith may be weak without your Savior being weak.
Your prayers may be trembling without God's throne trembling.
Your understanding may be incomplete without God's wisdom being incomplete.
Sarah's story does not teach us to glorify doubt.
It teaches us that God's faithfulness is not dependent upon human perfection.
And Hebrews 11:11 remembers Sarah in connection with faith, emphasizing that she considered Him faithful who had promised.
What a remarkable testimony.
Scripture records her laughter.
Scripture records her fear.
Scripture records her denial.
And Scripture also remembers her faith.
That is not because the Bible has forgotten her weakness.
It is because weakness was not the whole story.
God's grace had more to say.
Maybe that is what you need to hear today.
The worst moment of your life does not have to become the final definition of your life.
Your sin must be confronted, not romanticized.
Your wounds must be acknowledged, not denied.
Your losses must be grieved, not dismissed.
But in Jesus Christ, shame does not have to be your master.
There is forgiveness.
There is reconciliation with God.
There is a new life of discipleship.
There is grace that teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live for the One who gave Himself for us.
And there is a future resurrection hope that reaches beyond every limitation of this present world.
That is what we mean when we say:
Not that Jesus pretends our scandals never happened.
Not that every consequence instantly disappears.
Not that suffering automatically turns into worldly success.
But that through His death and resurrection, Jesus redeems sinners, transforms lives, and gives an eternal future to those who belong to Him.
And no human being is beyond His power to save merely because their history is ugly.
Think about the people who need to hear that.
The father who believes his failures have permanently destroyed his worth.
The mother who prays with tears after everyone else has fallen asleep.
The young adult secretly battling temptation while feeling unworthy to enter a church.
The believer who has drifted so far that returning feels humiliating.
The person who still carries the shame of something that happened years ago.
The exhausted Christian who has not stopped loving Jesus but has forgotten what spiritual rest feels like.
The seeker who wonders whether Christianity has anything to say to a life already filled with regret.
Perhaps one of those people is reading this right now.
Perhaps that person is you.
And perhaps God is using the truth of His Word to remind you that the question is not whether your circumstances look manageable.
The question is whether you know the One who is faithful.
That is why I want to ask you something personal.
Not as a test of how spiritual you appear.
Not as a demand that you reveal private details.
But as an invitation to honest reflection.
What have you quietly stopped bringing before God?
Is it your family?
Your spiritual life?
Your struggle with sin?
Your grief?
Your need for forgiveness?
Your fear about the future?
Or have you simply become so tired that you no longer know what to pray?
“Lord, help my unbelief.”
Those words come from Mark 9:24, where a father cried out to Jesus in the tension between faith and struggle.
Or “Christ is still healing me” if you are learning to walk with Him through wounds that have not fully healed.
You do not have to tell strangers everything you are carrying.
But you do not have to pretend that you are carrying nothing.
And when you see someone asking for prayer, do more than react to their comment.
Pray for them.
If appropriate, encourage them with Scripture.
Let the conversation become more than engagement.
Let it become a small expression of the body of Christ caring for one another.
Because the Church was never meant to be a gathering of people pretending they have no struggles.
It is a people redeemed by Christ, called to bear one another's burdens and walk together in truth and love.
And that brings me to something deeply important about why Gospel Warrior exists.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who will never voluntarily search for a sermon.
People who feel too ashamed to enter a church.
People who have never opened a Bible.
People who are one difficult night away from believing that their lives have no meaning.
People who have been wounded by false teaching and need to encounter Scripture explained faithfully.
People who have confused the failures of Christians with the character of Jesus Christ.
And people who simply need someone to point them back to the Gospel.
We cannot save them.
Only Jesus saves.
But we can proclaim His Word.
We can share the truth.
We can create resources that help people understand Scripture in context.
We can encourage believers toward repentance, prayer, worship, obedience, and deeper discipleship.
And we can keep reminding a wounded world that the cross and resurrection of Jesus Christ are not merely religious symbols.
They are the center of the Christian hope.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not building a personality around a platform.
Not turning spiritual pain into entertainment.
Not promising miracles in exchange for financial support.
But using the opportunities God gives us to make Christ known and help people grow in biblical truth.
You may never know who will read it.
Someone who has stopped praying.
Someone struggling with hidden guilt.
Someone who has been asking whether God still sees them.
Someone who needs to hear that forgiveness is found in Jesus Christ.
But it may place a biblical message in front of someone who would otherwise never encounter it.
And that is a meaningful reason to share.
Not because every sentence must be remembered, but because the Scriptures at its heart are worth returning to when circumstances make God's faithfulness difficult to see.
Our desire is to keep sharing daily biblical encouragement, Gospel-centered teaching, calls to repentance, testimonies of grace, and resources for deeper Christian discipleship.
We want believers who are serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ to have access to materials that encourage biblical study, prayer, spiritual maturity, and faithful Christian living.
And for those who feel led and are financially able to help sustain and expand this ministry, there is another way to partner with us.
For some supporters, that may be part of their broader practice of generous Christian giving.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful—not pressured or compelled.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
And that is exactly the spirit in which we invite you.
Not out of guilt.
Not because God needs your money.
And certainly not because a payment can purchase God's favor, forgiveness, or blessing.
Christ has already paid the price for our redemption through His own blood.
It can help us continue and expand.
It can support the development of future content and discipleship materials.
And it can allow this ministry to keep investing time and resources into serving the people who read, learn, and grow alongside us.
These products are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
They are simply another way to share encouraging messages and support the ongoing work.
The Gospel itself is not for sale.
The grace of God is not behind a paywall.
And the truth of Scripture belongs to everyone who comes to hear it.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Your faithful service in your own home, church, and community matters.
There are many ways to glorify God, and none of them should be reduced to a financial transaction.
Not merely as someone supporting content.
But as someone who values the ongoing work of helping others encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave this story, I want you to picture Sarah one final time.
Not the Sarah standing behind the tent.
Not the Sarah laughing because the promise sounded impossible.
Not the Sarah denying her laughter because she was afraid.
Picture the Sarah of Genesis 21.
An elderly mother.
Holding Isaac.
Looking at a child whose existence testified that God had done what He said He would do.
Imagine the weight of those years.
The memories.
The failures.
The disappointment.
The waiting.
And now, the child.
She could not recover all the years that had passed.
She could not undo the pain that had entered her household.
But she could see that the LORD had kept His word.
And somewhere in that moment, the question asked near the tent had received its visible answer.
“Is anything too hard for the LORD?”
No.
But perhaps the most important thing for you to remember is not that Sarah finally held Isaac.
It is that through the covenant story that continued after Isaac, God was moving toward a Savior who would offer something greater than one family's long-awaited joy.
Jesus Christ came to reconcile sinners to God.
And when He rose from the grave, He established a living hope that even death cannot destroy.
So if you are still waiting, do not confuse delay with proof that God has abandoned you.
If you are suffering, do not assume that your pain means you have failed to believe strongly enough.
If you have sinned, do not hide behind excuses when Christ calls you to repentance.
If you are weary, seek His grace, the encouragement of His people, and the help you need.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, do not mistake knowing Bible stories for knowing the Savior to whom Scripture points.
Come to Him.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Him.
Not because you can force God to give you the life you imagined.
But because in Jesus Christ, God offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life beyond anything this passing world can provide.
Sarah's laughter changed.
Her circumstances changed.
But the foundation of the story was never the strength of her emotions.
It was the faithfulness of her God.
And that is where I want to leave you.
With the God who heard a hidden laugh.
With the Savior who sees the hidden sinner.
With the cross where grace was purchased at immeasurable cost.
With the empty tomb where death's claim to ultimate victory was shattered.
And with a question that still reaches across the centuries into every heart tempted to believe that God has reached the limits of His power.
“Is any thing too hard for the LORD?”
Let your answer be shaped not merely by what you are hoping God will do tomorrow, but by what He has already accomplished through Jesus Christ.
“Jesus, I trust You with what I cannot understand.”
Because the greatest miracle is not that every broken dream will be restored in this lifetime.
It is that through Jesus Christ, people who were dead in sin can be made alive by grace.
And when the world has finished reminding you of everything that went wrong, remember the One who went to the cross to make sinners right with God.
Your past may explain the wounds you carry, but it does not have the authority to cancel the redemption Jesus Christ offers.
